# Enterprise HTML and CSS Architecture

## Purpose

Use this skill to design, review, or evolve HTML and CSS foundations for enterprise products, especially internal corporate applications and operational dashboards. It is intended for work where maintainability, semantic consistency, accessibility, performance, and governance must hold over time across multiple pages, teams, and release cycles.

## When to Use

- Defining or refactoring a front-end architecture for a new product, redesign, or large feature area.
- Structuring SCSS/Sass layers, partials, tokens, and component boundaries for long-lived products.
- Establishing design tokens, layout primitives, component boundaries, and naming conventions.
- Reviewing HTML and CSS for scalability, accessibility, responsiveness, or performance regressions.
- Creating governance rules for design-system adoption, code review, and long-term CSS maintainability.
- Standardizing page shells, content structure, and styling contracts before implementation begins.

## Do Not Use When

- The request is only about one isolated visual tweak or a tiny CSS bug fix.
- The main problem is framework-specific runtime logic rather than HTML/CSS architecture.
- The output is specifically HTML generated by VBA for Outlook; use `vba-html-vba` and `vba-css-vba`.
- The task is specifically about deterministic Node.js render pipelines; use `nodejs-html-css`.
- The primary need is a utility-first Tailwind strategy rather than layered enterprise CSS architecture.

## Related Skills

- `nodejs-html-css`: deterministic generation of HTML/CSS artifacts outside VBA.
- `vba-html-vba`: HTML generated inside VBA automation.
- `vba-css-vba`: constrained CSS for Outlook and VBA-generated markup.

## Non-Negotiable Rules

1. Treat HTML as the primary contract for semantics, accessibility, and content hierarchy.
2. Treat CSS as a layered system with explicit boundaries, not as page-local improvisation.
3. Define reusable tokens, primitives, and component rules before scaling page-specific styles.
4. Avoid selector strategies that depend on deep DOM nesting or brittle override chains.
5. Every layout and component decision must hold on narrow, medium, and wide viewports.
6. Accessibility and keyboard usage are first-class quality gates, not a later pass.
7. Performance budgets must influence architectural choices before visual polish.
8. New patterns must strengthen system consistency; do not add one-off exceptions without documented justification.
9. Prefer structured SCSS modules and partials only when they make ownership clearer; do not recreate cascade chaos inside Sass.

## Architecture Workflow

### 1. Define the Surface

Clarify the shape of the problem before writing markup or styles.

- Identify page types, shared shells, content density, and state complexity.
- Separate global concerns from feature concerns.
- List reusable UI primitives before identifying larger components.
- Record business-critical flows that cannot regress on mobile, keyboard, or reduced-motion contexts.

### 2. Model the HTML Contract

Build the semantic skeleton first.

- Establish heading hierarchy and landmark structure.
- Prefer native elements before introducing custom semantics.
- Define component states through stable attributes or classes, not visual-only markers.
- Keep document order aligned with reading order and keyboard expectations.

### 3. Define the CSS System Layers

Create explicit styling layers and keep responsibilities narrow.

| Layer | Responsibility |
| --- | --- |
| Tokens | Colors, spacing, typography scales, radii, shadows, z-index, motion values |
| Base | Resets, document defaults, typography, native element normalization |
| Objects | Layout primitives such as stack, cluster, grid, wrapper, and region |
| Components | Encapsulated UI patterns with explicit states and variants |
| Utilities | Small, intentional escape hatches for low-specificity overrides |
| Exceptions | Rare temporary rules with owner and removal intent |

For SCSS/Sass-first projects, keep the file structure aligned with those layers instead of organizing styles by page alone.

Recommended direction:

- `tokens/`: color, spacing, typography, elevation, motion, breakpoint, and z-index tokens.
- `base/`: reset, document defaults, typography, and element normalization.
- `objects/`: layout primitives such as stack, cluster, switcher, grid, shell, and region.
- `components/`: encapsulated UI building blocks with explicit variants and states.
- `utilities/`: intentional low-specificity helpers.
- `pages/` or `features/`: thin composition files only when page assembly is truly needed.

### 4. Choose the Right Styling Strategy

Use the simplest strategy that still scales.

| Situation | Preferred Direction |
| --- | --- |
| Shared product foundation | Design tokens plus layered CSS architecture |
| Repeated layout patterns | Object or primitive classes |
| Stable UI building blocks | Component-scoped classes with variant rules |
| Small alignment or visibility adjustments | Low-specificity utilities |
| Frequent theme switching | Token-driven theming with minimal component branching |

### 5. Establish Naming and State Rules

- Use names that describe role, not appearance alone.
- Keep state naming explicit, such as `is-open`, `has-error`, or semantic data attributes.
- Avoid names tied to temporary layout context.
- Keep selectors shallow and intention-revealing.
- Prefer composition over increasingly specific overrides.
- In Sass, use partials and modules to express ownership boundaries, not to justify deep selector nesting.

### 6. Design for Responsive Behavior Upfront

- Start with content constraints, not device labels.
- Use intrinsic layout techniques before breakpoint-heavy branching.
- Make overflow, truncation, wrapping, and empty states explicit.
- Confirm that spacing, line length, and tap targets remain acceptable under stress.

### 7. Make Accessibility a Build-Time Concern

- Verify landmarks, labels, heading order, focus order, and visible focus states.
- Ensure color choices meet contrast expectations in all supported themes.
- Preserve meaning when CSS fails or when custom fonts do not load.
- Respect reduced motion and avoid motion-only communication.

### 8. Control Performance Costs

- Budget for font loading, image strategy, animation cost, and CSS payload size.
- Avoid architecture that requires large override layers or dead styles to function.
- Prefer predictable layout behavior that minimizes cumulative layout shift.
- Treat render-blocking styles and unused CSS as architecture problems, not cleanup tasks.
- Limit Sass output growth by preventing duplicated imports, repeated variant generation, and theme explosion.

### 9. Govern Adoption

- Document which patterns are canonical, deprecated, experimental, or forbidden.
- Require new components to map back to tokens, primitives, and semantic contracts.
- Reject additions that duplicate an existing pattern with different naming.
- Define review criteria before a pattern spreads across the product.

## Decision Matrix

### Sass Architecture Decisions

| Question | Preferred Answer |
| --- | --- |
| Repeated design values across modules | Centralize as tokens or Sass maps with strict ownership |
| Shared layout pattern across screens | Promote to object layer instead of copy-pasting page selectors |
| Component variants growing too fast | Reduce variant surface and define a smaller API |
| Nesting required for readability | Keep it shallow and stop before coupling to fragile DOM depth |
| Page file getting large | Split by component or object responsibility, not by arbitrary chunks |

### HTML Decisions

| Question | Preferred Answer |
| --- | --- |
| Native element available | Use the native element first |
| Content order differs from visual order | Preserve semantic order and solve layout in CSS |
| State needs machine-readable hooks | Use data attributes or explicit state classes |
| Content repeats across pages | Create a stable structural contract before styling variants |

### CSS Decisions

| Question | Preferred Answer |
| --- | --- |
| Same value repeated many times | Promote it to a token |
| Same layout repeated in many contexts | Promote it to an object or primitive |
| Same UI pattern repeated with variants | Promote it to a component API |
| Rule exists only to beat another selector | Refactor architecture instead of increasing specificity |
| Pattern needs one local escape hatch | Add a utility only if the system boundary stays clear |

## Quality Gates

### Semantic Gate

- Landmarks, headings, lists, tables, and form relationships are correct.
- Reading order survives CSS changes.
- Component states have stable structural hooks.

### Accessibility Gate

- Keyboard navigation is complete and visible.
- Focus management is intentional.
- Contrast, reduced motion, zoom, and reflow behavior are acceptable.

### Performance Gate

- CSS payload and font strategy stay within agreed budget.
- Critical rendering path is not expanded without reason.
- Layout shifts and expensive effects are justified.

### Maintainability Gate

- Tokens, primitives, components, and utilities have clear boundaries.
- Selector specificity remains controlled.
- New code does not duplicate an existing pattern.

## Repo-Specific Constraints

- Prefer this skill for modern product HTML/CSS architecture and reusable front-end standards.
- Default assumptions should favor internal systems, dashboards, high-density information layouts, and long-lived maintenance.
- If the deliverable is generated from Node.js templates or dashboards in this repository, combine this skill with `nodejs-html-css` instead of replacing it.
- If the output targets Outlook or VBA-generated HTML, do not apply modern web assumptions blindly; route to the VBA-focused skills.

## Supporting Assets

- Use the [architectural review checklist](./references/review-checklist.md) when reviewing an existing implementation.
- Use the [design token starter template](./assets/design-tokens-template.md) when defining or standardizing tokens.
- Use the [architecture decision record template](./assets/html-css-adr-template.md) when formalizing a front-end architecture choice.

## Validation

1. Confirm the architecture defines tokens, primitives, components, and state rules explicitly.
2. Review one representative page for semantic landmarks, heading order, and keyboard flow.
3. Validate responsive behavior under narrow, medium, and wide content stress.
4. Verify that accessibility requirements are covered before visual refinements are accepted.
5. Check that selectors stay shallow and that overrides do not depend on accidental DOM depth.
6. Confirm that performance-sensitive choices such as fonts, animations, and CSS payload were considered.
7. For Sass projects, verify that partial organization matches ownership boundaries and that compiled CSS does not balloon due to duplication.

## Troubleshooting

| Symptom | Root Cause | Action |
| --- | --- | --- |
| CSS becomes harder to change every sprint | No clear layer boundaries or token strategy | Re-establish tokens, primitives, and component ownership |
| New pages copy styles with slight naming differences | Missing governance and canonical pattern registry | Create canonical patterns and block near-duplicate additions |
| Mobile layout breaks under real content | Layout built for screenshots rather than constraints | Rework primitives around intrinsic layout and content stress |
| Accessibility issues appear late | Semantics and focus behavior were deferred | Move semantic and keyboard checks into the first architecture pass |
| Too many overrides are needed | Specificity and component scope were not controlled | Simplify selectors and rebuild component boundaries |
| Performance regresses after redesign | Visual polish added without budget discipline | Revisit font, motion, asset, and CSS payload decisions |

## Pre-Delivery Checklist

- [ ] Semantic HTML contract is explicit and stable.
- [ ] CSS layers, tokens, and component boundaries are documented.
- [ ] Responsive behavior was designed from content constraints, not screenshots.
- [ ] Keyboard, focus, contrast, and reduced-motion expectations were reviewed.
- [ ] Selector specificity remains intentionally low.
- [ ] Performance-sensitive decisions were reviewed against a budget.
- [ ] Governance exists for introducing or rejecting new patterns.
